Martian expansion

120 original colors preserved. 1,024 colors in the expanded palette. An independent Gamut Forge extension of Warren Mars’s Martian Colour Wheel.

Mars adjusts hue spacing, shade/tint tone, and tint hue by eye. In his final revision, he restores vivid exemplars and lets them occupy different brightness rings. We use that final RGB table as the source of all 120 anchors.

48 hue families

The 24 original families alternate with 24 intermediates. Each has 13 shades and tints in the wheel and eight muted companions below it. White outlines identify the original RGB anchors. The wheel’s radius follows the ramp sequence; it is not a constant-lightness scale.

How this expansion is constructed
ComponentPer familyTotal
Five original ring positions and four midpoints9432
Two deeper shades and two lighter tints4192
Four tones × two muted saturation levels8384
Shared neutral grays—16
Total48 × 21 + 161,024

We interpolate shortest-arc HSV hue, saturation and value separately at each source ring. This carries the source’s hue bends into the new families. Each intermediate family also gets a fully saturated, full-value exemplar, placed at the nearest of the five ring lightnesses before the ramp is subdivided. This gives all 48 families a vivid peak without requiring those peaks to share a ring. Original RGB triples take precedence over the rounded HSV figures printed alongside them; all 120 are preserved exactly.

Two deeper shades multiply the darkest source value by 0.35 and 0.65. Two lighter tints multiply the lightest source saturation by 0.75 and 0.5. The four intermediate ring positions also provide muted companions at 0.4 and 0.7 times their saturation. Their hues bend toward the family’s lightest tint, and value is solved to preserve the parent’s linear-sRGB luminance before byte rounding.

Those extension formulas are ours. They approximate a continuation of the source’s decisions; they are not additional colors selected by Mars or a validated new perceptual model. Sixteen grays use evenly spaced CIELAB L* targets, including black and white.

RGB rounding produces no duplicates, so no fillers or individual color nudges are needed. Perceptual distances are measured but do not override the retained source anchors.
